title: AI Sovereignty and Global Interdependence: Navigating Industry Realities
gist: An ASPI Delhi roundtable summary argues that no country can control the full AI value chain, so India should define AI sovereignty as strategic autonomy and leverage its AI governance architecture via interoperable (not harmonized) frameworks, especially through BRICS. It flags gaps: cross-border data sharing, liability regimes, a still-vacant AI Safety Institute director post, and BRICS declarations that add infrastructure working groups but no new governance substance.

insights.claim: As of 2025 the global digital economy accounted for 17.3% of total global GDP.
insights.so_what: Sizes the economic stakes driving governments' push for sovereign AI.
insights.quote: As of 2025, the global digital economy occupies 17.3% of the total global GDP.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: A 2025 International Data Center Authority survey found that approximately 87% of the global industry considers AI a top priority.
insights.so_what: Broad corporate prioritization of AI supports sustained demand for AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: a 2025 International Data Center Authority survey asserts that approximately 87% of the global industry considers AI as a top priority
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: No single country controls the AI value chain: the Netherlands dominates lithography machines, Taiwan logic chips, South Korea memory chips, and the US and China lead in chip design and foundation models, making total AI sovereignty futile.
insights.so_what: Sovereign-AI ambitions will create cross-border dependencies rather than self-sufficiency, sustaining the moats of chokepoint suppliers.
insights.quote: attempts to have total control over the AI value chain are futile since it is not controlled by any single country
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: The 'AI sovereignty-interdependence paradox' describes the tension between desiring complete control over the AI infrastructure value chain and the reality that the chain relies on capabilities, capacities, and resources of multiple countries.
insights.so_what: A useful lens for judging which national AI strategies are realistic versus costly over-reach.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Experts argued India should define AI sovereignty as strategic autonomy, built by leveraging strengths and creating mutually beneficial dependencies, and invest patient capital in data repositories, application development, and talent retention.
insights.so_what: Points Indian AI policy toward applications, data, and talent rather than full-stack infrastructure self-sufficiency.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Because India lacks capabilities in AI infrastructure, semiconductor fabrication, and critical minerals, it must use its institutional capacity for AI governance as its lever for strategic autonomy.
insights.so_what: India's near-term AI edge is regulatory and institutional, not hardware; hardware dependence on foreign suppliers persists.
insights.quote: Since India does not have capabilities in AI infrastructure, semiconductor fabrication, or critical minerals, it must use its institutional capacity for AI governance to gain its strategic autonomy.
insights.locator: Since India does not have capabilities
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: India's November 2025 AI governance guidelines created a three-part architecture: the AI Governance and Economic Group for interministerial coordination, a Technology Policy Expert Committee for technical advice, and a hub-and-spoke AI Safety Institute for distributed safety research.
insights.so_what: India has a governance skeleton most countries lack, which could make it a reference model for the Global South.
insights.locator: India already has an architecture for AI governance
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: India should build a globally interoperable rather than harmonized AI governance framework, since interoperability preserves the state's ability to adapt rules to domestic social challenges.
insights.so_what: Expect India to resist adopting EU-style uniform rules while seeking compatibility for cross-border AI business.
insights.quote: India must further develop it into a globally interoperable governance framework, rather than making it a harmonized framework
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: India's AI Safety Institute director post, announced on May 19, 2026, remained vacant as of October 7, 2026, slowing progress on technical AI safety deliverables.
insights.so_what: Execution gaps weaken India's claim to lead Global South AI safety certification.
insights.quote: while the director post for India's AISI was announced on May 19, 2026, the position remains vacant as of October 7, 2026
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: India's AI Safety Institute has an opportunity to become the primary safety institute for the Global South by issuing certifications on data standards and governance calibrated to emerging economies.
insights.so_what: An Indian certification regime could become a market-access standard for AI vendors across emerging markets.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Roundtable experts recommended using existing ISO standards such as ISO 42001:2023 as the base for model-level AI governance, layered with multi-tiered sectoral standards for non-model aspects of AI systems.
insights.so_what: ISO 42001 compliance may become a baseline requirement for AI firms operating in India and allied markets.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Cross-border data sharing frameworks and liability regimes are the two key enablers of interoperable AI governance: data gives developers diverse datasets while liability rules provide legal certainty across the AI value chain.
insights.so_what: Watch liability and data-flow rules as the main regulatory variables for AI companies' cross-border operations.
insights.locator: To enable interoperable AI governance framework
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Implementing India's National Data Governance Framework is hampered because data generated or controlled by state governments is a sub-national subject, making uniform nationwide data-sharing practices hard to achieve.
insights.so_what: Federal fragmentation may slow the availability of population-scale Indian datasets for AI developers.
insights.locator: Navigating the Paradox Starts with Cross-Border Data Sharing
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Discussants proposed storing defense and critical-infrastructure datasets in air-gapped data centers while making non-personal data openly accessible via APIs as a national artifact.
insights.so_what: Implies demand for sovereign air-gapped data-center capacity alongside open government data platforms.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: India's AI Governance Guidelines call for a graded liability framework assigning responsibility by function performed and due diligence undertaken, and Singapore's Ministry of Law has issued a consultation paper on AI and intellectual property signaling an imminent liability framework.
insights.so_what: AI liability rules are arriving across Asia, affecting compliance costs and legal risk for AI deployers.
insights.locator: Developing Legal Certainty Through Liability Regimes
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

themes.theme: Diverging global AI governance and BRICS

insights.claim: The G7's 2025 AI for Prosperity statement pushes AI diffusion via cross-border data flows, while the 2025 BRICS statement stresses UN centrality and national sovereignty, so G7 diffusion efforts will run into BRICS sovereignty anchored in domestic law.
insights.so_what: Global AI markets are likely to fragment along G7 vs BRICS regulatory lines.
insights.quote: the push for AI diffusion through the G7 will meet the challenge of AI sovereignty and governance anchored on domestic legislations from BRICS members
insights.locator: To build such an interoperable AI governance
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Developing a BRICS framework for AI governance may yield more durable outcomes than pursuing universal AI standards.
insights.so_what: Suggests a bloc-based rather than global AI rulebook, raising compliance complexity for multinational AI firms.
insights.quote: developing a BRICS framework for AI governance may yield more durable outcomes than pursuing universal standards
insights.locator: BRICS does not contest AI diffusion
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Global AI governance frameworks are diverging rather than converging, as shown by the EU AI Act, China's World AI Cooperation Organization, Singapore's AI Verify, and the private-sector-led US approach.
insights.so_what: Regulatory fragmentation raises costs for AI companies and favors firms able to localize compliance.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: The 2026 BRICS Chennai Consensus created infrastructure-focused efforts, including a working group on high-performance computing and AI and a BRICS submarine cable network with its own maintenance vessels, which could speed AI diffusion and undersea-cable repair.
insights.so_what: A BRICS-owned cable and compute network would reduce dependence on Western-controlled digital infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: The 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration reaffirmed the 2025 BRICS AI governance statement but fell short of new initiatives, with no provisions on AI Safety Institute interoperability, cross-border data sharing, or AI liability.
insights.so_what: BRICS AI governance remains rhetorical; do not expect a binding bloc-wide AI regime soon.
insights.quote: it falls short on any new initiatives or progress since 2025
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
